blocks.title: Data Acquisition and Understanding
blocks.body:
All AI systems are built on data. The quality, diversity and provenance of that data shapes what the AI learns - and what biases, gaps or assumptions get embedded.

This stage of the AI lifecycle is where the principles of data ethics apply most directly. But there are additional considerations specific to AI: training data is often sourced at scale, from multiple origins, and can encode historical inequalities that the AI then perpetuates and amplifies.

blocks.title: If you use AI tools rather than build them
blocks.body: You can't audit the training data behind a tool like Copilot yourself - that's not your job, and you don't have access to it. But knowing that bias usually enters through how the data was collected, not through anyone deliberately programming discrimination in, changes how you read a tool's output. If it seems to perform less well for a particular group, task or context, that's usually why - worth treating as a signal to check further, not dismissing as a one-off glitch.

blocks.title: The frameworks suggest...
blocks.body:
The EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk AI systems to use training, validation and testing data that is relevant, sufficiently representative, and - to the best extent possible, given its intended purpose - free of errors and complete, taking steps to identify and address data biases that could lead to discriminatory outcomes. The Act doesn't define what 'complete' means in practice - it's an obligation to document and justify gaps in your data's coverage, not a bright-line test you can simply tick off.

UK GDPR applies to any personal data used to train AI models, including requirements around lawful basis, data minimisation and purpose limitation. Repurposing personal data to train an AI beyond the purpose it was originally collected for needs either a compatibility assessment against that original purpose, or a new lawful basis - and may be unlawful without one. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 has since relaxed the compatibility test further for certain purposes, such as research, archiving and statistics, but the underlying requirement to justify the new use remains for everything else.

blocks.title: Bias in data
blocks.body: The categories below broadly follow Suresh & Guttag's (2021) taxonomy of where bias enters a machine learning pipeline.

items.title: Historical bias
items.body: AI trained on historical data can encode the prejudices and inequalities of the past. If past hiring, lending or policing decisions were discriminatory, an AI trained on that data will learn to replicate those patterns - potentially at far greater scale.

items.title: Representation bias
items.body:
If certain groups are underrepresented in training data, the AI will perform less well for those groups. Facial recognition systems, for example, have been found to have significantly higher error rates for women and people with darker skin tones - NIST's 2019 Face Recognition Vendor Test found false-positive rates for some algorithms up to 100 times higher for West and East African and East Asian faces than for Eastern European faces.

Source: NIST FRVT Part 3: Demographic Effects (2019)

items.title: Measurement bias
items.body:
Measurement bias arises when a model optimises for a proxy - something easier to measure than what actually matters, but not quite the same thing. A widely used US healthcare algorithm used patients' past healthcare costs as a proxy for their health need, on the assumption that sicker patients cost more to treat. But less money is spent treating Black patients with the same level of need, so the algorithm systematically underestimated how sick they were, and under-referred them for extra care. Removing cost as the proxy and predicting illness directly eliminated the racial bias.

Source: Obermeyer et al., Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations, Science (2019)

items.title: Label bias
items.body: Bias can also arise from how data is labelled, not just what's measured. If the people labelling training data bring their own assumptions, those assumptions become embedded in the model - particularly important for subjective tasks like content moderation or sentiment analysis.

items.title: Aggregation bias
items.body: Treating a diverse population as homogeneous creates bias. An AI system designed around the 'average user' may systematically underserve people who differ from that average - including minority groups, older people, and people with disabilities.

blocks.title: Try it yourself: Spot the bias type
blocks.body:
Each short scenario below shows one of the bias types covered above. Try to name which one applies before revealing the answer.

  1. A. A bank's loan-approval model is trained on ten years of past lending decisions. It learns to approve fewer applications from postcodes that were historically redlined, even though postcode isn't used as an input.
  2. B. A voice assistant trained mostly on recordings from young adult native speakers performs noticeably worse at recognising older people's speech.
  3. C. A university's dropout-risk model is trained on lecturers' subjective notes on which students seemed 'engaged' in class, recorded differently by different staff.

first.alt: A magnifying glass, representing identifying a bias type in a scenario
first.body: Work through scenarios A, B and C above and decide which bias type - historical, representation, measurement, label or aggregation - best explains each one. Then select the button below to compare against one set of example answers.

second.alt: A clipboard with a checkmark, representing completed example answers
second.body:
A - Historical bias. The model reproduces a pattern from past decisions (redlining) even without being told the sensitive attribute directly - a classic proxy for historical discrimination.

B - Representation bias. Older speakers were underrepresented in the training data, so the model performs worse for them specifically.

C - Label bias. The 'ground truth' itself - what counts as 'engaged' - reflects each labeller's own subjective judgement, so that inconsistency gets baked into the model.

Real scenarios often show more than one bias type at once - the point of this exercise is building the habit of asking which one(s) apply, not memorising a single right label.

items.title: Where does your data come from?
items.body: The provenance of training data matters both ethically and legally. Data scraped from the internet, purchased from third parties, or drawn from legacy systems may have been collected without the knowledge or consent of the individuals it relates to. Understanding where your data came from - and on what basis - is a foundational responsibility.

items.title: Lawful basis and transparency
items.body:
Even where data was collected lawfully, using it to train an AI may not have been covered by the original basis it was collected under. Organisations need to consider whether individuals were informed their data might be used in this way, and whether they had a meaningful choice or a meaningful way to object. Consent is only one of six lawful bases under UK GDPR - organisations training AI on personal data more often rely on legitimate interests than consent, but the same transparency questions apply whichever basis they use.

This gets harder once a model has already been trained. Removing someone's data from a dataset is straightforward in principle; removing its influence from a model already trained on it - sometimes called machine unlearning - is a genuinely unsolved problem in many cases, not a checkbox to tick.

items.title: Synthetic and anonymised data
items.body:
Where consent or representativeness is a challenge, synthetic data - artificially generated data that mirrors real data's statistical properties - can help. However, synthetic data is not a silver bullet: it can still encode the biases present in the real data it was derived from.

Anonymised data is a separate approach - data stripped of identifying details so it falls outside data protection law entirely. This is harder to achieve than it sounds: re-identification research has repeatedly shown that data combined with other available information can often be traced back to individuals, meaning much data labelled 'anonymised' is really only pseudonymised, and remains personal data subject to the same protections.

items.title: Who prepared this data?
items.body: Behind most large training datasets is significant human labour: people who labelled, moderated, ranked or filtered the data an AI model learns from. This work is frequently outsourced to workers paid far less than equivalent roles in the country commissioning the AI, and can involve prolonged exposure to disturbing material. Responsible data sourcing has to consider not just what data was used, but who prepared it, and under what conditions.

items.title: Ask yourself
items.body:
• Do you know where your training data came from?
  • Was it collected on a lawful basis that covers its use in AI training?
  • Is your dataset representative of the people your AI will affect?
  • Have you checked for known sources of bias?
  • Do you know who prepared or labelled this data, and under what conditions?
  • If someone withdraws consent, can they be removed not just from the dataset but from any model already trained on it - and if not, do the people affected know that?

blocks.title: Case study: COMPAS
blocks.body:
COMPAS (Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions) is an algorithmic tool used in parts of the US criminal justice system to predict the likelihood of a defendant reoffending. Judges use its scores to inform sentencing and bail decisions.

An investigation by ProPublica in 2016 found that the algorithm was nearly twice as likely to falsely flag Black defendants as higher risk compared to white defendants - and nearly twice as likely to incorrectly label white defendants as lower risk.

The developers, Northpointe, disputed the findings: they argued COMPAS satisfied calibration (a given risk score means the same likelihood of reoffending regardless of race), while ProPublica's analysis focused on error-rate balance (false positive and false negative rates should be equal across groups). Both were right about their own metric. Research since has shown that whenever base rates differ between groups and predictions are imperfect - exactly the situation here - calibration and error-rate balance cannot both hold at once: it is mathematically impossible to satisfy every common definition of fairness simultaneously under those conditions (Kleinberg, Mullainathan & Raghavan 2016; Chouldechova 2017).

Source: ProPublica, Machine Bias (2016)

blocks.title: What does the COMPAS case reveal about fairness in algorithmic systems?
blocks.instruction: Select one option, then select Submit.

items.text: COMPAS was significantly more accurate at predicting reoffending than the judges who used it.
items.feedback: Not quite. COMPAS's developers didn't dispute that its risk scores could be biased - they disputed which definition of fairness mattered most. This case isn't about comparing the algorithm's accuracy to human judges.

items.text: Criminal justice data is too inconsistently recorded across jurisdictions to train a reliable predictive algorithm.
items.feedback: Not quite. Data quality and consistency weren't the issue here - COMPAS's data was usable enough to produce risk scores; the dispute was about which fairness definition those scores should be judged against.

items.text: Different mathematical definitions of fairness can conflict, so satisfying one can break another.
The system would have been fair if it had simply been trained on more data overall.
items.feedback: Not quite. More data wouldn't have resolved the tension - the disputed definitions of fairness can conflict with each other mathematically, regardless of how much data trains the model.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. COMPAS illustrates that there is no single, agreed definition of fairness in algorithmic systems - and meeting one definition often means violating another. Building fair AI is not just a technical challenge; it requires explicit ethical choices about which definition of fairness to prioritise, and for whom.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. COMPAS illustrates that there is no single, agreed definition of fairness in algorithmic systems. Meeting one definition often means violating another. Fairness in AI requires explicit ethical choices - not just better data or more sophisticated algorithms.

blocks.title: Case study: The human labour behind AI
blocks.body:
Not every data ethics issue is about the people an AI system is used on - some are about the people used to build it. Large AI models, especially generative ones, rely on vast amounts of human labour to label, moderate and rank training data, work that is often outsourced to lower-income countries and paid far below rates typical in the country where the AI company itself is based.

In 2023, an investigation revealed that OpenAI had used workers in Kenya, employed through an outsourcing firm, to label text for ChatGPT's safety systems - including graphic descriptions of violence, child sexual abuse and self-harm, so the model could learn to recognise and avoid producing it. Workers were reportedly paid between roughly $1.32 and $2 an hour, and several described lasting psychological harm from the material they were exposed to.

This was not an isolated case: similar labelling and content-moderation supply chains sit behind other major AI systems. Data provenance is not only a question of representativeness and consent - it also raises the question of who did the work of preparing the data, under what conditions, and for what pay.

blocks.title: What does this case reveal about the human labour behind AI systems?
blocks.instruction: Select one option, then select Submit.

items.text: Most of this kind of labelling work has since been fully automated using AI classifiers.
items.feedback: Not quite. This work still requires human judgement to review and label disturbing content accurately - it hasn't been automated away, and reporting continues to find human moderators behind similar systems today.

items.text: Labelling and moderation work is often outsourced to low-paid workers exposed to harmful content.
This was a temporary arrangement that ended once ChatGPT's initial safety systems were built.
items.feedback: Not quite. Reporting has found similar outsourced labelling and moderation arrangements are an ongoing, recurring part of how major AI systems are built - not a one-time exercise that later stopped.

items.text: The workers involved were paid at rates similar to equivalent roles in the company's home country.
items.feedback: Not quite. Workers were reportedly paid between roughly $1.32 and $2 an hour - far below rates typical for equivalent roles in the country where the AI company itself is based.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Responsible data practices don't end with checking a dataset for representativeness and consent - they extend to the conditions under which the data was prepared. Labelling and moderation work for AI systems is frequently outsourced to workers paid a fraction of rates typical in the commissioning company's home country, sometimes at real psychological cost.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. This work was performed by human workers, paid a fraction of the rates typical in the country where the AI company itself is based, and reporting has found this pattern is not limited to one company. Responsible data practices have to consider not just what data is used, but the conditions under which it was prepared.

blocks.title: Coming up...
blocks.body: With data acquired and understood, the next stage is Modeling - training, testing and evaluating the AI system. This is where algorithmic bias can emerge even from seemingly clean data, and where explainability, documentation and security testing become critical.
